summary:
Chile's Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019, applies in full to the Región Metropolitana de Santiago. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry, with no therapy or surgery required. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the statute's under-14 exclusion cannot stand as written: on 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, a ruling that applies only to that case.

Non-discrimination and hate-crime rules also apply nationwide. The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Transphobic violence is documented in Santiago and elsewhere. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, while the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Local authority practice across the capital's comunas diverges sharply, and a visitor's experience of municipal protection depends on which comuna they are in. On 15 April 2026 the Ñuñoa municipal council approved Chile's first anti-discrimination ordinance by nine votes to one; it bans hate speech, obliges non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, creates a communal good-practice seal and requires anti-exclusion notices in municipal buildings, and it was drafted by the comuna's Diversity and Non-Discrimination Department head María Fernanda Ulloa and endorsed by mayor Sebastián Sichel.
tangentialFactors:
Restrictive proposals are active at national level but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

Political retreat at municipal level is visible in the capital's affluent comunas. After committing to the LGBT rights organisation Movilh to raise the LGBT flag for the 17 May anti-homophobia date, the Vitacura municipality reversed under pressure from its republican councilors and refused to fly it, while neighbouring Santiago and Ñuñoa comunas participated. The refusal marks a municipal-level retreat, and it shows that symbolic protection withdrawn from one comuna can coexist with formal non-discrimination obligations in another.

Care policy remains unsettled for minors. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, and the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe.
